es.summary: La ERC es la pérdida progresiva y permanente de la función renal, evaluada por una disminución sostenida del filtrado glomerular. Diabetes e hipertensión son las causas más frecuentes.
key_points: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² por ≥3 meses indica ERC
Proteinuria >300 mg/día sugiere daño renal avanzado
Control estricto de presión arterial y glucemia ralentiza la progresión
Complicaciones comunes: anemia, enfermedad ósea‑mineral y desequilibrio electrolítico

pathophysiology: Hipertensión o hiperglucemia dañan nefronas → esclerosis glomerular
Disminución del número funcional de nefronas reduce GFR
Retención de sodio y agua eleva presión arterial, creando círculo vicioso
Acumulación de desechos (creatinina, BUN) produce toxicidad sistémica
risk_factors: Uso prolongado de AINEs o nefrotoxinas
signs_symptoms: Fatiga, debilidad y pérdida de apetito
Alteraciones del sueño por prurito o disnea
diagnostics: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (creatinina sérica mg/dL elevada)
Proteinuria >300 mg/dL en muestra de orina de 24 h
Ecografía renal: aumento de tamaño o pérdida de corteza
treatment: Inhibidores de la ECA (enalapril) o ARB (losartán) para controlar presión arterial
Diuréticos de asa (furosemida) para manejo de edema
Control glucémico con metformina u otros antidiabéticos
Dieta baja en sodio (<2 g/d) y proteínas (0.8 g/kg/d)
nursing_care: Monitorear presión arterial, frecuencia cardíaca y peso diario
Registrar balance hídrico y salida de orina cada turno
Evaluar mucosas, turgencia cutánea y edema
Revisar resultados de laboratorio (creatinina, eGFR, electrolitos)
Administrar medicamentos según prescripción y observar efectos adversos
Preparar al paciente para sesiones de diálisis si corresponde
patient_teaching: Seguir dieta baja en sodio y proteínas según indicaciones dietéticas
Tomar los antihipertensivos y antidiabéticos exactamente como se prescriben
Reconocer signos de empeoramiento: aumento de edema, falta de aliento, cambios en la orina
Evitar AINEs y suplementos de potasio sin autorización
Importancia de asistir a controles de laboratorio y consultas regulares

outcomes: Equilibrio electrolítico mantenido: K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L en 48 h

interventions.action: Monitorear niveles séricos de potasio, sodio y bicarbonato cada 24 h
interventions.rationale: Detectar alteraciones tempranas y prevenir arritmias

interventions.action: Evaluar ingesta y salida de líquidos y registrar balance cada turno
interventions.rationale: Mantener volumen adecuado que influye en electrolitos

interventions.action: Administrar diuréticos según prescripción y observar signos de hipopotasemia
Educar al paciente sobre alimentos ricos en potasio y sodio y su moderación
interventions.rationale: Control dietético ayuda a estabilizar electrolitos

interventions.action: Notificar al médico si K⁺ <3.5 mEq/L o >5.5 mEq/L

outcomes: Presión arterial estable ≥100 mmHg en 24 h
Peso corporal estable ±0.5 kg en 48 h
Hidratación adecuada: mucosas húmedas en 24 h

interventions.action: Registrar balance hídrico cada 8 h y comparar con órdenes
Administrar fluidos intravenosos según prescripción y monitorizar signos vitales
Evaluar piel y mucosas cada turno para detectar deshidratación
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana de déficit de líquidos

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre importancia de ingesta de líquidos y registrar consumo
Colaborar con el médico para ajustar dosis de diuréticos si es necesario

en.summary: CKD is the progressive and permanent loss of kidney function, assessed by a sustained decline in glomerular filtration rate. Diabetes and hypertension are the most common causes.
key_points: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months indicates CKD
Proteinuria >300 mg/day suggests advanced kidney damage
Strict control of blood pressure and glucose slows progression
Common complications: anemia, bone‑mineral disease, and electrolyte imbalance

pathophysiology: Hypertension or hyperglycemia damages nephrons → glomerular sclerosis
Reduction in functional nephron number decreases GFR
Sodium and water retention raises blood pressure, creating a vicious cycle
Accumulation of waste (creatinine, BUN) produces systemic toxicity
risk_factors: Prolonged use of NSAIDs or nephrotoxins
signs_symptoms: Fatigue, weakness, and loss of appetite
Sleep disturbances from pruritus or dyspnea
diagnostics: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (serum creatinine mg/dL elevated)
Proteinuria >300 mg/dL in a 24‑hour urine sample
Renal ultrasound: increased size or loss of cortex
treatment: ACE inhibitors (enalapril) or ARBs (losartan) to control blood pressure
Glucose control with metformin or other antidiabetics
Low‑sodium diet (<2 g/d) and protein (0.8 g/kg/d)
nursing_care: Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, and daily weight
Record fluid balance and urine output each shift
Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, and edema
Administer medications per prescription and monitor for adverse effects
Prepare patient for dialysis sessions if indicated
patient_teaching: Follow low‑sodium and protein diet as directed
Take antihypertensives and antidiabetics exactly as prescribed
Recognize signs of worsening: increased edema, shortness of breath, changes in urine
Avoid NSAIDs and potassium supplements without authorization
Importance of attending regular lab checks and appointments

outcomes: Electrolyte balance maintained: K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L within 48 h

interventions.action: Monitor serum potassium, sodium, and bicarbonate levels every 24 h
interventions.rationale: Detect early changes and prevent arrhythmias

interventions.action: Assess fluid intake and output and record balance each shift
interventions.rationale: Maintain adequate volume that influences electrolytes

interventions.action: Administer diuretics per prescription and monitor for hypokalemia
Educate patient on potassium‑rich and sodium‑rich foods and moderation
Notify physician if K⁺ <3.5 mEq/L or >5.5 mEq/L

outcomes: Stable blood pressure ≥100 mmHg in 24 h
Stable body weight ±0.5 kg in 48 h
Adequate hydration: moist mucous membranes in 24 h

interventions.action: Record fluid balance every 8 h and compare with orders
Administer intravenous fluids per prescription and monitor vital signs
Assess skin and mucous membranes each shift to detect dehydration
Educate patient on importance of fluid intake and record consumption
Collaborate with physician to adjust diuretic dosage if necessary

summary.1.quote: Diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes of CKD.

key_points.2.quote: Treatments cannot cure kidney disease, but they may slow kidney disease. They include medicines to lower blood pressure , control blood sugar , and lower cholesterol .

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Other major risk factors for kidney disease are (American Kidney Fund, n.d.): African, American Indian, or Asian heritage diabetes mellitus family history of kidney disease glomerulonephritis hypertension increasing age medication use (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics) obesity polycystic kidney disease pyelonephritis smoking urinary tract obstruction (e.g., urinary tumors, enlarged prostate, kidney stones) Pathophysiology o

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: Other major risk factors for kidney disease are (American Kidney Fund, n.d.): African, American Indian, or Asian heritage diabetes mellitus family history of kidney disease glomerulonephritis hypertension increasing age medication use (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics) obesity polycystic kidney disease pyelonephritis smoking urinary tract obstruction (e.g., urinary tumors, enlarged prostate, kidney stones) Pathophysiology o

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: If the disease progresses, the patient will begin to develop symptoms, which may include nausea and vomiting, fatigue, sleep disturbance, urinary changes, decreased cognition, muscle cramping, peripheral edema, pruritis (itching), resistant HTN, chest pain, and shortness of breath (CDC, 2022a).

sections.complications.5.quote: Common chronic diseases associated with the cardiovascular system include HTN, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, heart failure, valvular disease, and atrial fibrillation.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: As part of the assessment process, the nurse will closely monitor fluid balance through accurate recording of intake and output as well as electrolyte balance with regular assessments of kidney values, including serum creatinine and BUN levels, and GFR.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: It is important to closely monitor patients receiving diuretic therapy for electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hypokalemia), worsening renal failure, and hypotension , the latter two of which are common with the use of diuretics.

sections.nursing_care.5.quote: For patients with more severe or end-stage kidney disease, dialysis , or the use of a dialyzer machine to filter the blood and remove toxins when kidney function is decreased, is often indicated.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: The nurse should monitor the patient closely for signs of fluid overload, such as edema, shortness of breath, or crackles in the lungs.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: As part of the assessment process, the nurse will closely monitor fluid balance through accurate recording of intake and output as well as electrolyte balance with regular assessments of kidney values, including serum creatinine and BUN levels, and GFR.
